links.per: one percentage-point increase in TSP concentration relative to place start; local linear elasticity approximation near start
links.group: infant birth cohorts exposed to TSP; internal-cause deaths per live births
links.anchor: IV elasticity 0.45; reported design/subsample elasticity spread 0.3 to 0.7. Per pct-of-start point divide each elasticity by 100.
links.source: Chay and Greenstone 2003, Air Quality, Infant Mortality, and the Clean Air Act of 1970, NBER w10053, pp.20-21,26-27; https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w10053/w10053.pdf

research.result: Page 26: inverse-sampling-error-weighted IV elasticity 0.45. Pages 20 to 21 report 0.3 to 0.6; page 27 reports 0.6 to 0.7 near the regulatory cutoff.
research.breadth: US monitored counties, 1971 to 1972 changes induced by Clean Air Act nonattainment. TSP, not PM2.5 or an air-quality index. Outcome is internal-cause infant deaths per live births.
research.access: Working paper full text and tables read.
research.conversion: size = 0.45 / 100; range = [0.3 / 100, 0.7 / 100]. The cause is percent of starting TSP, so a one-point increase gives a 0.45% local proportional mortality increase.
research.transportLimit: Study specification/subsample spread is not a CI or modern PM2.5 coefficient. Requires TSP-specific cause and infant internal-cause outcome readers; neither was verified. No supported general air-quality-index conversion.
research.readerStatus: No person feels this yet: no cause or outcome reader was verified in this research batch. A numeric entry is not runtime activation proof.

chain: Clean Air Act nonattainment restrictions changed industrial emissions in monitored US counties.
Measured historical TSP concentrations fell under those restrictions.
The study used regulation-driven concentration changes to identify an effect on internal-cause infant mortality per live birth.
Most measured benefit occurred within one month of birth; fetal exposure is a suggested physical pathway, not a biologically isolated mechanism.
whyAnswers.bedrock: Regulatory constraints and measured physical TSP exposure. The biological mechanism remains a hypothesis; no person-level treatment or decision is inferred.
whyAnswers.reverseOnRepeal: Removing a restriction may change future emissions only if actual emitters respond. It cannot reverse a past birth exposure or death; causal symmetry at current PM2.5 levels is unproven.
whyAnswers.affected: Historical monitored county birth cohorts, 1971–1972; internal-cause infant deaths per live births. Not every current resident or all-cause mortality.
whyAnswers.lag: Study annual changes; greatest effect within one month of birth suggests prenatal exposure. Existing lagMonths=0 is not proof of an instantaneous individual hazard.
whyAnswers.placeVariation: Only a TSP-qualified exposure metric and matching cohort/baseline support this historical coefficient. No universal PM2.5 conversion.

causeMismatch.currentBaseUnit: population-weighted annual average PM2.5, micrograms per cubic meter, 2022–2024
causeMismatch.required: Separate historical-TSP input or researched transport coefficient/baseline; no assumed TSP/PM2.5 ratio.

personConsumer.existing: crisis person/mortality records and actual saved birth dates exist; TSP exposure-to-person and internal-cause infant outcome writer are not verified
personConsumer.rule: Read actual prenatal/residence exposure and age-under-one interval; preserve cause and stamp IDs on a real consequence. These saved infants have no verified TSP exposure or law-linked infant outcome; do not apply the coefficient or invent a death.
